title: The vowel points

objectives.can: Name the full vowel points and read a consonant with its vowel.

explanation.summary: The Hebrew Bible was first written with consonants alone. The vowels you see in a printed Bible are small marks, added later by the Masoretes, that fix the reading handed down in the community. This lesson teaches the eight full vowel signs and how to read a consonant together with its vowel.

sections.heading: Points added to a consonantal text
body: The twenty-two letters were enough for readers who knew the text. In the early Middle Ages, scribes called Masoretes added small marks, the vowel points (in Hebrew, niqqud), to record how the text was read aloud. Several systems of pointing were in use. The one printed in nearly every Bible today is the Tiberian system, named for the city of Tiberias.

So a pointed text is the consonantal text plus a layer of tradition. The consonants are the older layer. The points record a reading that is very careful, and they are what you learn in this course, but they were added to the letters, not written with them.

sections.heading: Eight full vowels
body: The first table lists the eight full vowel signs. Each consonant is read first and its vowel follows: a vowel sign belongs to the consonant it sits under, but its sound comes after the consonant's sound. So בָּרָא is read ba-ra: the qamets under the ב is read after the b, and the qamets under the ר after the r.

Six of the signs are placed below the letter: qamets, patah, tsere, segol, hireq and qibbuts (three slanting dots). Holem is a dot above and to the left of the letter. Shureq is a dot written inside a vav, which is then a letter of the word as well as a vowel sign. In the table the signs are shown on bet, except for shureq, which needs its vav.

sections.heading: Five classes, long and short
body: Traditional grammars arrange the vowels in five classes by the vowel sound: a, e, i, o and u. Each class has a long vowel and a short one, so that the sounds make partners: qamets and patah, tsere and segol, holem and qamets hatuf, shureq and qibbuts. The second table shows the pairs. Hireq stands alone in the table because it can be short, as in most words, or long, when a yod follows it.

This is the traditional school scheme. Modern Hebrew keeps five vowel sounds and does not mark length at all, so qamets and patah sound alike there, and so do tsere and segol. Scholars debate how far length was a real difference in the Tiberian pronunciation, and also what the vowels actually sounded like. For reading, the signs are what matters.

sections.heading: Qamets and qamets hatuf
body: One sign, the qamets, stands for two vowels. Most of the time it is the long a (qamets). In some syllables it is a short o and is then called qamets hatuf, 'the shortened qamets'. The two look the same on the page. You can tell them by the syllable they stand in: qamets hatuf stands in a closed syllable that carries no stress, as in the word כָל when it is joined to the next word by a short line. Lesson H0.3.1 teaches syllables, and until then you need only know that the problem exists.

sections.heading: Vowels written with letters
body: A holem or a hireq is often followed by a vowel letter that supports it. A holem with a vav, written וֹ, still reads as o. Lesson H0.3.1 teaches these vowel letters in full. Shureq is the one vowel that is always written with its vav.

misunderstandings: The vowel signs are not letters. A word like בָּרָא has three consonants, however many marks it carries.
The sign stands under its consonant, but it is pronounced after it: ב with qamets is ba, never ab.

A dot above a letter can be a holem or the dot of shin or sin, and a dot inside a letter is a dagesh or a shureq. Look at what the letter is: a dot inside a vav is shureq; a dot inside another letter is a dagesh (lesson H0.2.3).
Qamets and qamets hatuf are one sign. You cannot tell them apart by looking at the sign alone.

deeper.heading: Other systems of pointing
body: The Tiberian pointing was not the only one. Babylonian and Palestinian systems placed the signs above the letters and differ in their details. They show that the vocalisation of the Bible was a tradition worked out at a particular time, with competing forms. The Tiberian system, with its fuller records, won out and is the one printed in Hebrew Bibles.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בָּרָא has three consonants and a qamets under the first two: the reading is ba-ra. The dot inside the bet is not a vowel, it is a dagesh (lesson H0.2.3). The second word, אֵת, has a tsere, two dots side by side below the alef: the consonant is read first, then its vowel.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: אֶת has a segol, three dots in a triangle below the alef. כִּי has a hireq, one dot below the kaf, followed by the consonant yod. The dot inside the kaf is a dagesh; the hireq is the dot below it.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: In וְחֹשֶׁךְ the first full vowel is a holem, a dot above and to the left of the het. The next syllable has a segol under the shin. The word beside it, עַל, has a patah under the ayin: a short horizontal line.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Here a holem is written with a vav: the dot stands above the vav, and the whole is read as o. The word is alef, vav, resh. Compare shureq, a dot in the middle of a vav, which is read as u.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him to the ark, for the waters were on the face of the whole earth; and he put forth his hand, and took her, and brought her in unto him into the ark.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The qamets under the kaf of כָל looks like the qamets of בָּרָא, but here it is a short o: the word is read kol. The syllable is closed and carries no stress, because the word is tied to the next by the short line after it. This is qamets hatuf.

reading.why: Three verses that between them contain every vowel sign of the lesson except the qibbuts: qamets, patah, tsere, segol, hireq, holem and shureq. Read each consonant and then its vowel; do not try to translate yet.
